Members One of Another
MEM-burz WUN uv uh-NUTH-ur
n. phr. (the mutual belonging of believers as limbs of one body)
Greek melēethe allēlōn — melos, a limb or member of the body, and allēlōn, of one another. The English member here keeps its older anatomical sense of a bodily limb.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Paul uses the phrase twice. In Romans: “So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another.” In Ephesians it grounds a command about speech: “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.” The English word member has weakened into a term for someone enrolled on a list, but the Greek melos means a limb, and the whole argument depends on the stronger sense. Believers are not members of a church the way men are members of a club, by subscription and at will; they are limbs of a body, joined by life and not by decision, and a limb has no existence apart from the body it belongs to. Paul develops the figure at length in the first Corinthian letter: “For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.” Two consequences follow in the apostle's own reasoning. Difference is necessary rather than regrettable, since a body made of one kind of limb is not a body. And injury is shared, so that lying is forbidden on the ground stated — a man who deceives his brother is a hand deceiving its own body. The phrase is therefore not a sentiment about warm fellowship but a statement about what the church is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Key Scripture

Rom 12:5 — "So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another."

Eph 4:25 — "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another."

1Co 12:12 — "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ."

1Co 12:26 — "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."

Modern Corruption

Church membership has been reduced to a voluntary affiliation held at will, so a phrase describing limbs of one body is read as a description of a club's roster.

expand to see more

The consumer model of church life is the direct contradiction of this phrase. A congregation is approached as a provider of services to be evaluated and exchanged, attendance is kept provisional, and formal membership is declined as unnecessary or treated as a mere formality. The arrangement is defended on the ground that the church is people rather than an institution, which is true and beside the point, since Paul's figure is not institutional but organic and binds more tightly rather than less. A limb does not evaluate its body. The same instinct produces the unattached Christian who follows teaching online and belongs nowhere in particular, which on this figure is not a reduced form of church life but a severed limb.

The error has a counterpart that must be named as well, because the figure cuts both ways. Leaders who use body language to demand compliance, to suppress legitimate dissent, or to make departure from a congregation feel like apostasy have taken Paul's organic image and used it as a chain. Nothing in the passage supports that. The apostle's own applications are protective of the weaker member and insistent that the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee. The principle to recover is mutual belonging with teeth: that truth-telling is owed because we are limbs of one body, that the suffering of one member is the suffering of all, and that this belonging is created by union with Christ rather than by joining.
